guidingQuestion: In what ways do people depend on healthy ecosystems, and what happens to us when those ecosystems change?
hook: Clean tap water, a crunchy apple, and the grassy dune between a beach town and a storm all depend on living systems working quietly in the background, so what happens when one part of that system stops working?

keyIdeas: An ecosystem service is a natural process of a healthy ecosystem that people benefit from, such as cleaning water, building soil, pollinating crops, or softening floods. Nature also supplies natural resources: ecosystems grow wood, food, and the starting chemicals for many medicines, while stone and metals come from Earth's rocks and minerals.

Services come from the ordinary work of living things: decomposers turn dead organisms back into soil nutrients, pollinators carry pollen between flowers, and soil and wetlands filter water as it passes through. Matter cycles, while energy passes through and leaves as heat.

Biodiversity is a service too. Wild populations hold a variety of traits, and some of those traits resist disease. A crop grown as one uniform variety across huge areas lacks that variety, so scientists turn to wild relatives for resistance traits to develop new varieties.

A small change in one part of an ecosystem can set off big changes somewhere else. When a livestock drug wiped out most of India's vultures, carcasses the vultures no longer ate fed growing numbers of feral dogs, and more people were bitten and exposed to rabies.
Coastal dunes, marshes, and beach grasses take the force of storms and slow erosion. Building over them removes that protection; restoring them can bring it back.

Engineers judge solutions by criteria (what success requires) and constraints (limits such as cost and environmental impact). New York City met its needs by protecting the upstate watersheds that clean its water naturally instead of building a huge new filtration plant.

Money is only one way to measure what ecosystems are worth. People also value them for recreation, wildlife, beauty, and future discoveries, so good decisions weigh evidence and the needs of many stakeholders.

glossary.definition: A natural process carried out by a healthy ecosystem that people benefit from, such as filtering water, building soil, pollinating crops, or softening floods.
A material or energy source that comes from nature and that people use, such as wood, stone, minerals, water, food, or plant chemicals used to make medicines.
The movement of nutrients such as nitrogen from the soil into living things and back again, mostly as decomposers break down dead matter.
An organism, such as a fungus or many kinds of bacteria, that breaks down dead organisms and wastes and returns their nutrients to the soil.
The transfer of pollen to a flower so the plant can make seeds and fruit; for many plants, animals such as bees, butterflies, and moths do the carrying.
The variety of life in a place, including how many different species live there and how much individuals of the same species differ in their traits.
A trait that makes an organism less likely to be infected by, or to die from, a particular disease.
An animal that feeds on organisms that are already dead instead of hunting and killing its own food.
Describes an animal of a tame kind, such as a dog or cat, that lives on its own with no owner caring for it.
The wearing away and carrying off of soil, sand, or rock by moving water, wind, or ice.
An area of land where rain and melting snow drain into the same set of streams, rivers, wetlands, and lakes.
The requirements a design must meet to count as a successful solution.
A limit a design must work within, such as cost, available materials, or its effects on people and the environment.
A person or group affected by a decision, who has something to gain or lose from how it turns out.

explorer.title: A Living Workforce You Never See
paragraphs: Turn on a faucet, bite into an apple, or walk across a wooden floor, and you are using something an ecosystem helped make. Scientists call the natural processes that healthy ecosystems carry out for people ecosystem services.

Some services are easy to picture: bees moving pollen, wetlands trapping mud and germs, dune grass gripping sand during a storm. Others are quieter, like soil forming over many years, forests holding carbon in their wood, or wild plants containing chemicals that may become tomorrow's medicines.

Nature also hands us natural resources, the raw materials people use. Living ecosystems grow wood, food, and medicine chemicals and help keep water clean; stone and metals are dug from rocks that formed over long spans of geologic time, not grown by living things. And some services feed the mind more than the body: hiking a mountain trail, studying a coral reef, or simply enjoying a meadow all count.

diagram.caption: One way to sort the sixteen services on the lesson's wheel, plus two resources from Section 1
diagram.alt: A table sorting the sixteen ecosystem services on the lesson's wheel into four groups, plus two resources named in Section 1. Supplies materials: food and chemicals for medicines, plus wood and fresh water from Section 1. Keeps the system running: pollination, decomposition, soil formation, nutrient recycling, photosynthesis, biodiversity. Regulates and protects: water purification, air purification, erosion or flood control, pest control, carbon storage. Enriches human life: recreation, appreciation of nature, scientific discovery.

Pollination, decomposition, soil formation, nutrient recycling, photosynthesis, biodiversity
Water purification, air purification, erosion or flood control, pest control, carbon storage
Recreation, appreciation of nature, scientific discovery

explorer.watchOut: An ecosystem service is something the ecosystem does for people, not a chore people do for the ecosystem. Sorting services into neat groups is just one way to organize them: pollination keeps the system running and supplies food at the same time.

explorer.title: How the Work Gets Done
paragraphs: In a mountain meadow, flowers pull nutrients from the soil, grasshoppers munch the leaves, and sooner or later everything dies. Fungi and bacteria then break down the remains, releasing nutrients such as nitrogen into the soil where new roots can take them up. Over many seasons this builds deep, rich soil, and the same recycling keeps a farm's own soil fertile.

Bees and butterflies visiting flowers for food get dusted with pollen and carry it to the next flower. That delivery lets many plants make fruit and seeds, including apples, squash, almonds, and blueberries. The big grain crops, wheat, rice, and corn, are mostly pollinated by wind or by themselves.

Water gets cleaned on the move. As rain soaks through soil and creeps through wetlands, particles settle out and some wastes are broken down. Healthy ecosystems do much of this work, though people still usually filter or disinfect water before drinking it.

Biodiversity works like an insurance policy. Individuals in a wild population differ in their traits, so when a new disease arrives, some may resist it. Scientists borrow those traits from wild plants to breed crops that can fight disease.

diagram.caption: Matter cycling in a meadow (arrows show where matter goes next)
diagram.alt: A cycle diagram with five boxes. Meadow plants lead to dead plant matter when they die or shed leaves. Dead plant matter leads to decomposers (fungi and bacteria), which eat and break it down. Decomposers lead to nutrients in the soil, which they release, and also to carbon dioxide in the air, released by respiration. Meadow plants also release some carbon dioxide to the air through respiration. Nutrients in the soil lead back to meadow plants through their roots, and carbon dioxide in the air leads back to meadow plants through photosynthesis.

explorer.watchOut: Decomposers recycle matter, not energy. The nutrients in a dead leaf can be used again and again, but the energy stored in it is passed along and changed, and at each step some spreads out as heat that leaves the ecosystem. Sunlight keeps supplying new energy. Also, not every crop needs animal pollinators: the main grains are pollinated by wind or by themselves.

explorer.title: When One Piece Slips
paragraphs: In the 1990s, farmers in India began treating livestock with a cheap painkilling drug. It was safe for the cattle, but vultures that fed on the carcasses (dead bodies) of treated animals died. Within roughly a decade, several common vulture species had nearly vanished.

Vultures had been the cleanup crew. Without them, carcasses fed growing numbers of feral dogs, and dogs spread most human rabies cases, so more dogs meant more bites and more rabies. Nobody had listed disease prevention as a vulture job until the job stopped getting done.

Farms can set up the same kind of chain. When a huge area grows just one crop variety, every plant shares the same weaknesses, so one disease can sweep through. The banana most stores sell is a single variety, and its plants are genetic copies of one another. That variety is now threatened by newer fungal diseases.

Coasts show it too. Dunes held together by beach grass, and marshes along the shore, take the force of storm waves. Bulldoze them for roads and buildings, and floodwater reaches homes more easily, especially as sea level rises.

diagram.caption: A ripple of causes and effects (arrows point from cause to effect)
diagram.alt: A chain of six boxes, each causing the next: a livestock drug harmful to vultures is used; vultures die and their numbers crash; more carcasses are left for other scavengers; feral dog numbers grow; more people are bitten by dogs; more people are exposed to rabies.

explorer.watchOut: Two trends happening at the same time do not by themselves prove that one caused the other. Later studies compared health records from parts of India that had been home to many vultures with places that had few, and found that human deaths rose where vultures disappeared. More dogs and rabies are one likely pathway; dirtier water and disease from rotting carcasses are others.

explorer.title: Engineering With Nature
paragraphs: Engineers start by pinning down the problem. Criteria are what a solution must achieve; constraints are the limits it must respect. For New York City, the water had to be clean, plentiful, and able to serve a growing population, and the plan had to stay affordable over time and protect the environment.

Building a huge new filtration plant would have cost a great deal and, the lesson argues, might still have fallen behind a growing city. Instead, the city invested in protecting the upstate watersheds whose forests, soils, streams, and wetlands clean the water naturally. The water is still disinfected and constantly tested, but most of it does not need to be filtered.
Coastal towns use the same idea when they replant beach grass, rebuild dunes, and limit building on fragile shores. Restoring the ecosystem restores the service.

Real decisions involve trade-offs and stakeholders: families who need water, farmers, builders, people who fish or watch birds. Comparing costs helps, but a price tag misses values like recreation, beauty, and future discoveries, so good choices weigh evidence and many points of view.

diagram.caption: New York City's two options checked against its criteria and constraints (ratings follow the lesson's reasoning)
diagram.alt: A table comparing two water-supply options, with ratings that follow the lesson's reasoning. Clean, safe water (criterion): a huge new filtration plant, yes; protecting the watershed, yes, with disinfection. Enough water for millions (criterion): both yes. Treatment keeps up as the city grows, as the lesson argues (criterion): filtration plant unlikely; watershed likely. Affordable over time (constraint): filtration plant no, costly to build and run; watershed yes, lower cost. Protects the environment (constraint): filtration plant weak; watershed strong.
rows: Treatment keeps up as the city grows (as the lesson argues)
No: costly to build and run

explorer.watchOut: Natural solutions are not magic. A watershed only cleans water while it stays healthy, so it needs protection and monitoring, and the drinking water still gets disinfected. Choosing nature over machines is a design decision backed by evidence, not a rule that always wins.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 1 (p. 377) says that without pollinators, farmers could not produce the fruits, seeds, grains, and nuts they grow. Staple grains such as wheat, rice, and corn are wind-pollinated or self-pollinating, so this overstates pollinator dependence; many (not all) crops need animal pollinators. The same page also lists oranges and green beans among bee-visited farm crops and says some favorite foods rely on pollinators; green beans are self-pollinating, and Navel and Valencia oranges can set fruit without pollination.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says pollinators help many plants and many food crops reproduce, especially fruits, nuts, and vegetables. The seed question (Q08) keeps 'many' and rejects 'every crop'. Q09 sorts crops using the National Research Council report: apples, squash, almonds, and blueberries rely heavily on animal pollinators; wheat, rice, and corn do not. The O2 card and its watchOut name the grain exception. No content or question uses oranges or green beans as pollinator-dependent crops.

evidence.supports: Natural resources such as wood, stone, minerals, water, foods and medicine chemicals come from ecosystems; decomposers such as fungi break down dead organisms and release nutrients, building soil that farms need season after season; pollinators such as bees, butterflies and moths carry pollen between flowers, many plants depend on them, and bees supported by a meadow also visit crops such as apples and squash.

evidence.title: Status of Pollinators in North America, Chapter 4: Effects of Variations in Pollinator Populations on Pollination Services
evidence.publisher: National Research Council, The National Academies Press (2007)
evidence.supports: Staple grains such as rice, wheat and maize are self-pollinating or wind-pollinated, while crops such as almonds, apples, blueberries and cucurbit squashes depend heavily or completely on animal pollination; apples are self-incompatible and need cross-pollination between cultivars, not just between trees.

evidence.title: Which Garden Vegetables and Fruits Need Insect Pollination
evidence.publisher: Montana State University Extension (Bees in the Big Sky)
evidence.supports: Green, snap and string beans have self-pollinating flowers and need no insect pollinators, while apples and summer and winter squashes need insects for cross-pollination.

evidence.title: Oranges for Southern Arizona (az1850)
evidence.supports: Navel and 'Valencia' oranges can set fruit without the need for pollination.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 2 (p. 379) says Cavendish bananas are safe from Panama disease and that yellow sigatoka leaf spot makes Cavendish plants sicken and die when its spores arrive. This is dated and mixed up: Cavendish resisted the older Race 1 of Panama disease (Fusarium wilt) but is susceptible to Tropical Race 4, the wilt now killing Cavendish plantations; yellow Sigatoka is a leaf-spot disease that cuts photosynthesis and bunch size and has been largely displaced by black leaf streak. The text also says Panama disease drove other banana varieties to extinction; Gros Michel was largely abandoned by the export trade, not lost, and smallholder farmers still grow it.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says Cavendish resisted an older strain of Panama disease but newer fungal diseases now threaten it, and never names yellow sigatoka as the killer. Questions Q13-Q15 test only the supported principle: genetically uniform crops share weaknesses, and wild biodiversity supplies resistance traits. The clonal (genetic copy) point in Q13 is backed by Zheng et al. 2018. No content claims that a banana variety went extinct. Q13 asks about the supply of store bananas rather than the world's bananas, and Q14's key says wild traits help develop new resistant bananas.

evidence.locator: 2. Ecosystem Change Impacts Human Food Supplies—Bananas
evidence.supports: Individuals in natural populations differ in traits, and some traits help them survive a disease; disease resistance makes infection less likely; crops grown as one variety over large areas (Cavendish bananas) have low diversity, so scientists search wild bananas for disease-resistant traits.

evidence.title: New Geographical Insights of the Latest Expansion of Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense Tropical Race 4 Into the Greater Mekong Subregion (Zheng et al., 2018)
evidence.supports: Cavendish replaced Gros Michel because it resisted Race 1 of Fusarium wilt (Panama disease), but Cavendish clones are susceptible to Tropical Race 4; clonal propagation and low diversity raise the crop's genetic vulnerability.

evidence.title: Tropical race 4 - TR4
evidence.supports: TR4 is the strain of the Fusarium wilt fungus that readily causes disease in Cavendish bananas; it has devastated Cavendish plantations in several countries and cannot be controlled with fungicides.

evidence.title: Sigatoka leaf spot
evidence.supports: Yellow Sigatoka (Sigatoka leaf spot) is a fungal leaf-spot disease that lowers the leaf's photosynthesis and bunch size; it has been largely displaced by black leaf streak in many production areas.

evidence.title: Gros Michel
evidence.supports: Gros Michel was replaced by Cavendish cultivars in the export trade because of its susceptibility to Fusarium wilt, but it has not disappeared: smallholder farmers still grow it, in backyard gardens and mixed cropping systems.

reviewFlags.issue: Figure 3 (p. 381) is titled as if vulture declines cause the rise in feral dogs, and its caption says rabies cases rose as a result, but the graph plots only two time series (vultures 100% to 3%, feral dogs about 17 to 30 million, 1992-2004); no rabies data are shown. The figures are estimates from the time the textbook was written. The textbook's rabies-only story also simplifies later findings: a comparison of districts that had been vulture habitat with districts where vultures were rare found human death rates rose by more than 4 percent where vultures vanished, through a broad sanitation shock, with more dogs and rabies one likely pathway; that study measured human deaths, not dog numbers.
reviewFlags.resolution: No question reuses the textbook's graph numbers. Q19 uses clearly labelled model data and teaches the pattern only; Q20 asks what extra evidence would support cause (a comparison of places with and without vulture loss, the kind of comparison Frank and Sudarshan made for human death rates), and its explanation says that study measured human deaths. The O3 card's watchOut separates correlation from cause and names the later findings and their several pathways. The overall chain is supported by Markandya et al. 2008.

evidence.locator: Section 3. Vultures and Rabies, including Figure 3
evidence.supports: A veterinary drug used on cattle was linked to vulture deaths and the near-loss of three vulture species; more carcasses went to feral dogs, dog numbers rose, and because dogs carry rabies more people were infected; Figure 3 plots vulture numbers falling and feral dog numbers rising from 1992 to 2004; the lost, unrecognized service was disease prevention.

evidence.title: Counting the cost of vulture decline: An appraisal of the human health and other benefits of vultures in India (Markandya et al., Ecological Economics, 2008)
evidence.supports: Livestock use of the drug diclofenac caused sharp vulture declines in India; dogs, the main source of human rabies there, also eat carcasses and increased alongside the decline; the authors estimate a significant rabies-related health cost.

evidence.title: New research: The cost of species extinction – Evidence from the collapse of vultures in India
evidence.publisher: University of Warwick, Department of Economics
evidence.supports: Comparing data from before and after diclofenac was widely adopted, in areas where vultures had previously thrived, researchers found human death rates rose by more than 4 percent; extra dogs and rats spreading disease and rabies are suggested as one possible pathway.

evidence.title: The Social Costs of Keystone Species Collapse: Evidence from the Decline of Vultures in India (Frank and Sudarshan, American Economic Review 114(10), 2024)
evidence.supports: The functional extinction of India's vultures, after a cheap painkiller came into wide use on livestock, was a large negative shock to sanitation that raised human mortality by over 4 percent.

evidence.title: How does the loss of vultures lead to 500,000 people dying?
evidence.supports: Economists compared human death statistics in districts that had been vulture habitat with districts where vultures were not previously found: death rates rose in the former after diclofenac spread in the mid-1990s but not in the latter. Rabies-vaccine sales rose from 1996, and more feral dogs feeding on carcasses is offered as a possible, not proven, pathway.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 3 (p. 381) calls rabies 'a fatal disease for humans' without qualification. Rabies is virtually always fatal once symptoms appear, but it is preventable with prompt care after an exposure; dogs cause about 99% of human cases.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content describes rabies as a dangerous disease spread mostly by dog bites and gives no medical advice. No question tests whether rabies is always fatal.

evidence.locator: Section 3. Vultures and Rabies, including Figure 3
evidence.supports: The text calls rabies fatal for humans and says dog bites are how most people in India catch it; a veterinary drug used on cattle was linked to vulture deaths, more carcasses went to feral dogs, dog numbers rose, and more people were infected.

evidence.title: Rabies (fact sheet)
evidence.supports: Dog bites and scratches cause about 99% of human rabies cases; once symptoms appear rabies is virtually always fatal, but deaths are preventable with prompt post-exposure care.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 4 (p. 383) says flooding is now the leading cause of property loss and fatalities from natural disasters in the United States. FEMA supports 'most common and most expensive', but the National Weather Service ranks heat as the leading weather-related killer, ahead of floods.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content calls floods among the most common and costly U.S. disasters and makes no claim about fatality rank. No question tests this statistic.

evidence.supports: The text says coastal flooding has grown more common and more devastating and calls flooding the top cause of U.S. natural-disaster property losses and deaths; it adds that communities restore flood protection by restoring dunes, planting beach grasses, using river diversions and limiting coastal development.

evidence.title: Cost of Flooding
evidence.supports: Flooding is the most common and most expensive natural disaster in the United States.

evidence.title: Heat Safety
evidence.supports: Heat is the leading weather-related killer in the United States, causing more deaths per year than floods, lightning, tornadoes and hurricanes combined (2004-2013 averages: about 123 heat deaths versus 75 flood deaths per year).

reviewFlags.issue: Section 5 (pp. 384-385) simplifies New York City's story: it presents watershed protection as replacing treatment and implies the water needs little treatment. In fact the Catskill/Delaware supply has run under EPA filtration-avoidance waivers since 1993, kept through watershed protection, and the water is still disinfected (chlorine is added). The population and gallons-per-day figures are as of the textbook's writing. The text frames the problem as overloaded treatment plants; the Catskill/Delaware supply was unfiltered, and the real choice was building a new filtration plant (required by federal rules) or protecting the watershed to qualify for filtration avoidance. The p. 384 caption also says wetlands upstream were protected, but the watershed is mostly forest, along with farms, streams, wetlands, and reservoirs.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says watershed protection lets most of the supply skip filtration while the water is still disinfected and monitored. Q12 and Q26 reject 'no treatment needed'. No question tests the population or volume numbers. The O4 card, its table, key idea 6 and Q26 now name a huge new filtration plant as the alternative, and the O4 card and Q26 say forests, soils, streams, and wetlands clean the water. The O4 table labels the 'keeps up as the city grows' row as the lesson's argument about treatment.

evidence.locator: Section 5. Clean Drinking Water for New York City (introduction and caption)
evidence.supports: The text says the city's water treatment plants were stretched beyond their limits in the early 1990s as the population grew, and the caption says wetlands upstream were protected to filter the city's water naturally.

evidence.locator: Section 5. Use Ecosystems to Clean Water
evidence.supports: Larger treatment plants were expensive and unlikely to meet long-term needs; engineers instead protected the watersheds that naturally clean the city's water, which saves money and protects ecosystems; scientists monitor the water quality.

evidence.title: Filtration Avoidance Determination
evidence.publisher: New York City Department of Environmental Protection
evidence.supports: Since January 1993 the Catskill/Delaware supply has met the criteria for waivers from federal filtration requirements, kept in place through source-water (watershed) protection programs.

evidence.title: History of New York City's Drinking Water
evidence.publisher: New York City Department of Environmental Protection
evidence.supports: Chlorine is added to New York City's water to kill bacteria; the Croton system normally supplies about 10 percent of the city's water.

evidence.title: Drinking Water
evidence.publisher: New York City Department of Environmental Protection
evidence.supports: More than 1 billion gallons of water a day are delivered from upstate reservoirs to about nine million customers.

evidence.title: History of the New York City Watershed Filtration Avoidance Determination
evidence.publisher: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 2 (archived document)
evidence.supports: Under the Surface Water Treatment Rule a surface supply must be filtered unless it qualifies for filtration avoidance, which requires meeting water-quality limits, keeping disinfection in place and running a watershed control program. EPA found in 1993 that New York City met the criteria, so the Catskill/Delaware system is an unfiltered supply protected by land acquisition, watershed rules and farm programs, while the Croton system must be filtered.

evidence.title: Review of the New York City Watershed Protection Program (2020), Chapter 10: Ecosystem Protection and Management Programs
evidence.publisher: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (The National Academies Press)
evidence.supports: Forests cover about 70 to 90 percent of the land in the six West-of-Hudson (Catskill/Delaware) reservoir watersheds and act as a living filter for New York City's water.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 1 (p. 377) says decomposers use the energy and matter in dead organisms and release nitrogen and carbon-based molecules into the soil. Read literally, this could suggest energy is recycled into soil; much of the carbon also returns to the air as carbon dioxide through respiration.
reviewFlags.resolution: Q07, the O2 card (cycle diagram in which decomposers and plants both release CO₂ by respiration) and its watchOut state that matter cycles while energy is passed along and leaves as heat, consistent with the brief's guardrail.

evidence.supports: The text says decomposers such as fungi draw on both the energy and the matter in dead organisms and release nitrogen- and carbon-containing molecules into the soil, building the soil that crops need season after season.

evidence.title: Biology 2e, 46.3 Biogeochemical Cycles
evidence.supports: Energy flows through ecosystems and leaves as heat while matter is recycled; respiration returns organic carbon to the air as carbon dioxide; decomposers convert nitrogen in wastes and dead matter into ammonium in soil.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 4 (p. 382) says coastal marshes, swamps, and dunes 'absorb water' that would otherwise flood communities. This simplifies how they work: marshes and dunes mainly act as barriers that take up wave energy, slow water, and hold sediment.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says dunes and marshes take the force of storm waves and slow water and erosion. Q23 rejects the idea that dune plants soak up all floodwater.

evidence.supports: Coastal marshes, swamps and dunes reduce flooding risk; healthy beach grasses reduce storm impact and erosion; building towns and roads destroys these ecosystems so they can no longer provide the service, and rising sea level adds to the threat.

evidence.title: What is a living shoreline?
evidence.supports: Marshes and oyster reefs act as natural barriers to waves (15 feet of marsh can absorb about half of incoming wave energy), and living shorelines are more resilient in storms than bulkheads.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 1 (p. 377) says building materials such as wood, stone, minerals, and metals come from Earth's ecosystems. Stone, metals, and most minerals form through geological processes in Earth's crust, not through the activity of living things; they are natural resources but not ecosystem products, and ecosystem-service frameworks do not count them. The p. 377 caption also says the meadow builds and protects the soil farmers need, which loosely implies the meadow's soil reaches the farm; a farm's fertility comes from decomposers in its own soil.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content separates resources grown by living ecosystems (wood, food, medicine chemicals) from stone and metals dug from rocks formed by geology: key idea 1, the O1 card's third paragraph and its table. Q04's choice c rationale and explanation are fixed. Q03 now asks about services from healthy ecosystems near farms, with decomposers building fertile soil, and the O2 card says the same recycling keeps a farm's own soil fertile.

evidence.locator: 1. Healthy Ecosystems Provide Services (text and meadow caption)
evidence.supports: The text says natural resources include minerals, water and wood, and that building materials such as wood, stone, minerals and metals come from Earth's ecosystems; foods and medicine chemicals come from ecosystems; the caption says the meadow builds and protects soil that farmers need.

evidence.title: Mineral Resource Science—Supporting Informed Decisionmaking (Fact Sheet 2016–3034)
evidence.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey, Mineral Resources Program
evidence.supports: People use mineral resources to build homes and cities; mineral deposits form in Earth's crust, where regional geologic processes control where they form and how they are distributed, often buried beneath rocks and sediments.
